VOXEU COLUMN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FRONTIERS OF ECONOMIC RESEARCH
Letting AI agents write econometric code
Sebastian Galiani  Federico A. López  Raul A. Sosa / 18 Oct 2026

Large language models increasingly write the code behind empirical research. This column reports a benchmark of 40 econometric tasks in Stata, R, and Python. For each task, two leading models write a script, as a chatbot that never runs it and as an agent that runs and revises it. Letting the models run their code raises the share of correct results from 79% to 97% and makes the prompt and the software matter far less. The failures that remain under the agent come from scripts that run without errors but return wrong numbers, and detecting them is still the researcher’s work.

AUTHORS
Sebastian Galiani
Federico A. López
Raul A. Sosa
SHARE
Twitter
Facebook
LinkedIn
Bluesky

Economists are debating what artificial intelligence will do to their own research. Weder di Mauro (2026) argues that AI is raising the supply of competent papers while the number of slots in the top five journals remains fixed. Vansteenkiste (2026) suggests that AI may make the researcher’s role less about having the right answers and more about asking the right questions. Much of that debate is about how research is judged and what role remains for the researcher. This column concerns a more mechanical layer, the code that turns a dataset and a method into an estimate.

Code written by people has never been free of errors. An audit of 110 studies recently published in prestigious economics and political science journals finds coding errors in about a quarter of them, and such errors can be present even when the posted code reproduces the published numbers exactly (Brodeur et al. 2026). Economists often delegate estimation code to research assistants, and delegation does not remove the need to review it. Large language models can now write this code, and, like assistants, they can introduce such errors. Each generation of AI coding tools increases the volume of code that developers produce, while their software releases rise by far less, in part because AI-written code still has to be reviewed, tested, and integrated by people (Demirer et al. 2026).

Many users interact with language models through a chat window (Chatterji et al. 2025, Johnston et al. 2026) where, if the model answers with a script, the researcher must run it and request any corrections. Coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex are programs that surround the model, execute what it writes, and let it read the output and revise its code until it decides that it is finished. Korinek (2025) shows how economists can use such agents and build their own research agents. In a recent paper (Galiani et al. 2026), we ask how moving from a chat window to a coding agent changes the correctness of econometric code and what this implies for empirical researchers.

From chat window to coding agent

Ash and Hansen (2023) called for evaluating language models on the tasks that economists use them for, and econometric coding is one such task. We built a benchmark of 40 econometric tasks covering linear regression, difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, discrete choice, survival analysis, and time series. Each task states the method and comes with a simulated dataset and a reference output computed in advance. A run succeeds when the numbers it reports match that reference within a tolerance. We ran every task in Stata, R, and Python, with and without an example of a related task in the prompt, and under three degrees of agency, which differ in how much of the running and revising falls to the model.

Under the chatbot, the model writes one script and never sees it run. Under self-repair, we run the script and, if it fails to execute or its output lacks a required value, return the output so that the model can revise the script, up to three times. Under the constrained agent, so called because it has only a command line and its prompt confines it to the task, the model runs and revises its code as often as it chooses, is instructed to verify its calculation with an independent check, and decides when it is finished. We repeated every combination 10 times with each of two models, Claude Sonnet 4.6 in Claude Code and GPT-5.6 Luna in Codex, for 14,400 runs in total.

Task success rises with agency

Claude Sonnet 4.6 returns a correct result in 81.4% of chatbot runs, 93.5% of self-repair runs, and 99.2% of agent runs, while GPT-5.6 Luna moves from 77.3% to 90.3% and then to 95.1%. Self-repair, with at most three revisions, already achieves 68% of the agent’s improvement over the chatbot for Claude Sonnet 4.6 and 73% for GPT-5.6 Luna.

Figure 1, which pools the two models, shows that the prompt and the software matter less as agency increases. An example in the prompt (Brown et al. 2020) raises task success under the chatbot by 5.8 percentage points for Claude Sonnet 4.6 and 7.3 points for GPT-5.6 Luna but adds 0.7 and 1.5 points under the agent (Panel A). The choice of software shows the same pattern (Panel B). Under the chatbot with no example, Stata trails Python by 25.5 percentage points for Claude Sonnet 4.6 and by 30.8 points for GPT-5.6 Luna. Yet Stata is the most widely used software in empirical economics (Vilhuber et al. 2020). Under the agent with no example, the gap falls to 1.3 points for Claude Sonnet 4.6 and 6.8 points for GPT-5.6 Luna.

Figure 1 Task success by agency condition

Notes: Both panels pool the two models. Panel A averages over the three software environments and compares prompts with an example of a related task (one-shot) and without one (zero-shot). Panel B averages over the two prompts and compares Stata, R, and Python. Whiskers are 95% intervals from 4,000 draws of a cluster bootstrap over the 40 tasks. 
Source: Galiani et al. (2026).
Loud and silent failures

We call a failure loud when the script does not run or returns no complete output, so that the researcher sees an error message or a missing result. We call it silent when the script runs and returns its output, but at least one of the numbers it reports is wrong, so that nothing in the output flags the error. More than two-thirds of the silent failures whose scripts we read come from a coding error in an otherwise correct method, such as a wrong index or a wrong term in a formula. Under the chatbot, most failures are loud. The example mainly reduces loud failures, and Stata scripts produce them far more often than scripts in R or Python. The agent removes loud failures in all three environments, so that few failures remain for the example to prevent and most of the Stata gap closes.

Pooled over the two models, loud failures fall from 15.8 per 100 runs under the chatbot to zero under the agent. Silent failures fall from 4.9 to 2.9 per 100 runs (Figure 2). Total failures therefore fall from 20.7 to 2.9 per 100 runs, and every failure that remains is silent. The fall in silent failures comes almost entirely from Claude Sonnet 4.6, from 4.7 to 0.8 per 100 runs, against 5.1 to 4.9 for GPT-5.6 Luna. Under the agent, the task with the most failures is shift-share instrumental variables, where every failing run returns all its estimates but reports a standard error outside the tolerance.

Figure 2 Loud and silent failures by agency condition

Notes: Both panels pool the two models, the two prompts, and the three software environments, with 4,800 runs in each agency condition. Panel A shows loud and silent failures per 100 runs. Panel B shows the share of failures that are silent, and the second line of each label gives the number of failing runs. Whiskers are 95% intervals from 4,000 draws of a cluster bootstrap over the 40 tasks. No run fails loudly under the constrained agent, so the loud rate and the silent share have no interval there. 
Source: Galian et al. (2026).
The cost of agency

Running and revising code requires additional model calls, valued here at API list prices. For Claude Sonnet 4.6, the mean cost of a run rises by a factor of 3.1 between the chatbot and the agent, from 4.56 to 14.09 cents. For GPT-5.6 Luna, the factor is 5.0, but an agent run still costs less than one cent on average. The median agent run also takes 5.8 times as long as the median chatbot run for Claude Sonnet 4.6 and 3.4 times as long for GPT-5.6 Luna. For Claude Sonnet 4.6, each correct result that the agent adds over the chatbot costs about $0.54. At research-assistant wages of $15 to $50 an hour, this amount pays for 0.6 to 2.2 minutes of an assistant’s time.

Implications for empirical researchers

For a researcher choosing how to use these tools, the degree of agency matters more, on average, than the prompt or the software, whose effects fall sharply once the model can run its code. Delegating the running and revising of the code to the model removes the errors that are cheapest to detect. It removes only about two-fifths of those that the output does not flag, which the researcher must find by checking whether the model implemented the requested specification and whether its numbers are right. Rerunning the code would not reveal such errors, since, as Brodeur et al. (2026) note, code can reproduce the published numbers and still be wrong.

If researchers move from chat windows to coding agents, they encounter fewer errors, and a larger share of those errors is silent. Vansteenkiste (2026) argues that when accurate results grow harder to tell apart from plausible but inaccurate ones, journals should require more transparency about code and data. Weder di Mauro (2026) expects that as AI generates the technical analysis behind policy advice, what will stay scarce is a human relationship built on trust and accountability. Our results suggest a similar division of labour in empirical research, since agents run and revise the code at little cost but leave the researcher to judge whether its numbers are right.

References

Ash, E and S Hansen (2023), “Large language models for economic research: Four key questions”, VoxEU.org, 27 July.

Brodeur, A, D Mikola, N Cook, L Fiala, T Brailey, R Briggs, A de Gendre, Y Dupraz, J Gabani, R Gauriot et al. (2026), “Reproducibility and robustness of economics and political science research”, Nature 652(8108): 151–156.

Brown, T B, B Mann, N Ryder, M Subbiah, J Kaplan, P Dhariwal, A Neelakantan, P Shyam, G Sastry, A Askell et al. (2020), “Language models are few-shot learners”, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33: 1877–1901.

Chatterji, A, T Cunningham, D J Deming, Z Hitzig, C Ong, C Y Shan and K Wadman (2025), “How people use ChatGPT”, NBER Working Paper 34255.

Demirer, M, L Musolff and L Yang (2026), “Writing code versus shipping code: Productivity effects across generations of AI coding tools”, VoxEU.org, 21 June.

Galiani, S, F A López and R A Sosa (2026), “AI agents and prompt engineering in econometric coding”, NBER Working Paper 35588.

Johnston, D, D Holtz, A M Richmond, C Ong, P Tambe and A Chatterji (2026), “The shift to agentic AI: Evidence from Codex”, arXiv:2606.26959.

Korinek, A (2025), “AI agents for economic research”, NBER Working Paper 34202.

Vansteenkiste, I (2026), “Plus ça change. AI and the future of economic research: From Galileo back to Socrates”, VoxEU.org, 9 September.

Vilhuber, L, J Turitto and K Welch (2020), “Report by the AEA Data Editor”, AEA Papers and Proceedings 110: 764–775.

Weder di Mauro, B (2026), “AI, the future of economic research and of the many-handed economist”, VoxEU.org, 17 July.

VOXEU COLUMN MACROECONOMIC POLICY
Fiscal consolidation: Temporary costs versus lasting scars
Luiz de Mello  Joao Tovar Jalles / 17 Oct 2026

Public debt is at or near record highs across the OECD, increasing the pressure on governments to restore fiscal sustainability over time. This column draws on new cross-country evidence showing that the output costs of fiscal consolidation are modest and short-lived on average, and that lasting scars are hard to detect. But averages conceal a critical asymmetry: consolidations launched in high-debt environments are markedly more contractionary, and in more than half of the episodes in the sample the debt ratio was still higher three years after consolidation. Initial fiscal conditions matter more for outcomes than the choice between spending cuts and tax increases.

SHARE
Twitter
Facebook
LinkedIn
Bluesky
AUTHORS
Luiz de Mello

Director Organisation For Economic Co-operation And Development (OECD)

Joao Tovar Jalles

Senior Associate Professor of Economics University Of Lisbon

General government gross debt in the OECD area is around 112% of GDP, more than 40 percentage points above its pre-2008 average, while ageing, defence and climate commitments continue to add to spending pressures (OECD 2026, IMF 2026). Consolidation needs are sizeable in most advanced economies, motivating policy discussions about what fiscal tightening does to the economy.

The debate has long been organised around separate questions. One literature asks how much output is lost in the short run and finds that multipliers are larger in recessions and when monetary policy cannot offset the tightening (Auerbach and Gorodnichenko 2012, House et al. 2020). A second literature asks whether consolidation leaves permanent marks on productive capacity through lower public investment, weaker capital accumulation and hysteresis in labour markets (Fatás and Summers 2018). A third asks whether tightening can be self-defeating, raising rather than lowering the debt-to-GDP ratio because the denominator falls faster than the numerator (Attinasi and Metelli 2017, Castro et al. 2015).

These questions are rarely answered together, and that separation matters for policy. A government deciding when and how to consolidate needs to know not only the size of the immediate hit to activity, but also whether the adjustment leaves the economy structurally poorer, and whether it delivers the debt reduction it was designed to achieve. In a new paper (de Mello and Jalles 2026a), we address the three questions within a single empirical framework for a panel of advanced, emerging-market and low-income economies over 1970-2024.

Identifying consolidation without the narrative record

Identification is the central difficulty. Fiscal policy responds to the cycle, so raw changes in the cyclically adjusted primary balance (CAPB) partly reflect economic conditions rather than discretionary decisions. Narrative datasets solve this by reconstructing the policy record, but they exist for a limited set of countries and years (DeVries et al. 2011, Adler et al. 2024).

We use a three-layer strategy designed to travel across a wide cross-section. First, the primary balance is cyclically adjusted, and a fiscal reaction function is estimated in which the CAPB responds to lagged debt and to slow-moving structural controls; its residual is our measure of unanticipated consolidation. Alternatively, discrete and persistent consolidation episodes are dated using a multiple structural break procedure. Effects are then estimated with local projections for short-run dynamics, augmented with leads of the shock to allow for anticipation, and with panel dynamic OLS and an error-correction model for long-run relationships.

The episodes so identified look plausible. High-income economies account for the largest number, while upper-middle-income economies have the largest average adjustment, at about 2.5 percentage points of GDP. Expenditure-based and mixed packages together make up over 90% of episodes; purely tax-based adjustments are rare. Growth typically falls sharply before consolidation starts, from about 3.4% three years ahead of the episode, and then stabilises, underscoring that consolidation episodes often occur against a backdrop of prior economic weakness.

Short-run costs are real but fade

Our baseline local projections indicate that a one-percentage-point consolidation shock lowers the level of real GDP per capita on impact and keeps it below baseline for about two years, after which the loss steadily shrinks. By the third year the estimated response is effectively zero, and point estimates turn mildly positive thereafter. 

The long-run picture is less settled than the impulse responses alone would suggest. Dynamic OLS estimates point to a small negative association between consolidation and the long-run level of output, on the order of 1% to 1.3% of GDP per percentage point of adjustment, and the error-correction term is negative and highly significant. But these estimates are sensitive to how consolidation is measured: the negative coefficient is strongest when all positive CAPB changes are treated as shocks and disappears when narrative episodes are used. 

Taken together, the evidence of temporary demand-side costs is far stronger than that of permanent supply-side scarring.

When does consolidation reduce debt?

Whether consolidation improves debt dynamics is a separate question. In debt-dynamics regressions the coefficient on consolidation is negative at different horizons and grows in absolute size over time, consistent with tightening lowering the debt ratio; the interaction with lagged growth is insignificant, so the average relationship does not appear to depend much on initial cyclical conditions. The estimates are not statistically precise, however, and the confidence bands around the conditional marginal effect include zero throughout.

The episode-level count is more sobering. Among consolidations for which three-year debt outcomes are observable, 290 episodes, or 56% of the sample, saw the debt-to-GDP ratio rise within three years, against 228 debt-reducing episodes. Debt outcomes following consolidation therefore vary considerably across episodes, reflecting, among other factors, the interest-growth differential and initial economic conditions.

Debt levels, not instruments, drive the differences

Estimating the local projections separately for economies entering consolidation with high and low public debt, measured relative to the median lagged debt ratio among consolidation observations, produces two very different trajectories (Figure 1). 

Where initial debt is low, the output response hovers near zero and becomes mildly positive after three years. Where initial debt is high, output falls on impact and stays below baseline within a five-year horizon, with no sign of recovery. Interaction regressions confirm the pattern: the coefficient on the shock itself, which captures the low-debt case, is small and insignificant at every horizon, while the interaction with high debt is consistently negative and significant through the second year.

One possible mechanism is intuitive. Heavily indebted economies may face tighter financing conditions, higher risk premia and less room to cushion adjustment with other policy instruments, so a given tightening may bite harder and for longer. It is also precisely in these economies that consolidation is least avoidable, which is the uncomfortable core of the result.

Figure 1 Output effects of fiscal consolidation under high and low public debt

Notes: Estimated impulse response of real GDP per capita to a one-percentage-point fiscal consolidation shock, shown separately for countries with high and low initial public debt. High debt is defined relative to the median lagged debt-to-GDP ratio among consolidation observations. The vertical axis measures the cumulative percentage deviation of real GDP per capita from its pre-shock level; shaded areas are 90% confidence intervals based on Driscoll-Kraay standard errors. Sample period: 1970-2024. 
Source: de Mello and Jalles (2026a).

Impulse responses estimated separately for spending-based and tax-based episodes differ in their point estimates, with tax-based adjustments looking somewhat more favourable over the horizon, but the confidence bands overlap so heavily that no difference can be identified. That is a departure from the classic finding that expenditure-based adjustments are the more growth-friendly option (Alesina and Perotti 1997, Alesina et al. 2019), and it should be read as an absence of statistical resolution rather than as a refutation. The substantive point is comparative: initial fiscal conditions explain more of the heterogeneity in consolidation outcomes than the instrument mix does.

Implications for future adjustment

Three lessons follow for governments preparing to tighten. First, the short-run output cost of consolidation is not the binding argument against it. Losses are modest, they dissipate within about three years, and the evidence for permanent damage to productive capacity is weak. 

Second, timing and initial conditions dominate. Because consolidation is substantially more contractionary when debt is already elevated, the results strengthen the case for rebuilding fiscal buffers before debt reaches those levels. This complements our earlier finding that rigid spending structures, and large public wage bills in particular, reduce the likelihood of consolidation and push adjustment towards cuts in public investment (de Mello and Jalles 2026b).

Third, consolidation is neither the costless virtue of the expansionary-austerity literature nor the self-defeating trap of its critics. It is a policy whose payoff depends on when it is undertaken and how much fiscal room remains, and the evidence suggests that this room is best created well before it is needed.

References

Adler, G, M C Allen, G Ganelli and D Leigh (2024), “An Updated Action-Based Dataset of Fiscal Consolidation”, IMF Working Paper No. 2024/210.

Alesina, A and R Perotti (1997), “Fiscal adjustments in OECD countries: Composition and macroeconomic effects”, IMF Staff Papers 44(2): 210-248.

Alesina, A, C Favero and F Giavazzi (2019), Austerity: When It Works and When It Doesn’t, Princeton University Press.

Attinasi, M G and L Metelli (2017), “Is fiscal consolidation self-defeating? A panel-VAR analysis for the euro area countries”, Journal of International Money and Finance 74: 147-164.

Auerbach, A J and Y Gorodnichenko (2012), “Measuring the output responses to fiscal policy”, American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 4(2): 1-27.

Castro, G, R M Félix, P Júlio and J R Maria (2015), “Unpleasant debt dynamics: Can fiscal consolidations raise debt ratios?”, Journal of Macroeconomics 44: 276-294.

de Mello, L and J T Jalles (2026a), “Fiscal Consolidation: Temporary Costs or Lasting Scars?”, REM Working Paper No. 0431-2026, University of Lisbon.

de Mello, L and J T Jalles (2026b), “The role of spending rigidity in fiscal adjustment”, VoxEU.org, 12 March 2026.

DeVries, P, J Guajardo, D Leigh and A Pescatori (2011), “A New Action-Based Dataset of Fiscal Consolidation”, IMF Working Paper No. 2011/128.

Fatás, A and L H Summers (2018), “The permanent effects of fiscal consolidations”, Journal of International Economics 112: 238-250.

House, C L, C Proebsting and L L Tesar (2020), “Austerity in the aftermath of the Great Recession”, Journal of Monetary Economics 115: 37-63.

IMF (2026), Fiscal Monitor: Fiscal Policy under Pressure: High Debt, Rising Risks, International Monetary Fund.

OECD (2026), OECD Economic Outlook, Volume 2026 Issue 1, OECD Publishing.

VOXEU COLUMN FINANCIAL REGULATION AND BANKING POLITICAL ECONOMY
Never let a good crisis go to waste: Term limits and banking reforms
Orkun Saka  Yuemei Ji  Clement Minaudier / 17 Oct 2026

Financial crises routinely trigger sweeping overhauls of financial regulation, but whose interests do these reforms serve? Using data on financial policies in 88 democracies between 1973 and 2015, this column shows that leaders facing a binding term limit roll back financial liberalisation roughly three times more than leaders who can run again – but only in the wake of a financial crisis. The reforms they enact tend to favour incumbent banks over the general public. The effect is concentrated in countries where revolving doors between politics and finance are common, brings post-government career benefits to policymakers, but leads to no gains in banking stability.

AUTHORS
Orkun Saka
Yuemei Ji
Clement Minaudier
SHARE
Twitter
Facebook
LinkedIn
Bluesky

Financial crises are an endemic feature of market economies (Reinhart and Rogoff 2009). Their costs are severe – deep recessions, collapsing banking systems, and surging public debt – and they almost always prompt governments to rewrite the rules of the financial system. A long tradition in political economy sees this as a silver lining: crises weaken entrenched interest groups and open a window for necessary reforms (Drazen and Grilli 1993). The advice often attributed to Winston Churchill, to never let a good crisis go to waste, captures this optimistic view.

But the same advice can be taken by those with narrower goals in mind. Whether the policies introduced after a crisis serve the general population or incumbent financial institutions remains an open question. In a new paper (Saka et al. 2026), we argue that the answer depends crucially on whether politicians can still be held to account at the ballot box.

Crises could strengthen or weaken accountability

Elections are a key mechanism to keep politicians acting in voters’ interests. Leaders who can seek another term must satisfy voters, while leaders facing a binding term limit cannot be punished at the next election. A large literature documents that this matters for policy, from taxation and spending by US governors (Besley and Case, 1995) to corruption among Brazilian mayors (Ferraz and Finan, 2011).

How crises interact with this mechanism is theoretically ambiguous. On the one hand, crises put financial regulation in the spotlight. Greater salience means more voter scrutiny, which should push politicians up for re-election towards policies that benefit the public. On the other hand, crises flood legislatures with activity, make information noisier, and mobilise special interests. Lobbying intensifies precisely when the stakes are highest, and the rewards that the financial industry can offer politicians who deliver favourable policies – including lucrative post-office jobs (Blanes i Vidal et al. 2012) – rise accordingly. Such windows of opportunity are most valuable to politicians whose careers no longer depend on voters.

Comparing term-limited leaders with those eligible for re-election, before and after crises, allows us to see which of these forces dominates.

Four decades of financial policies

We combine two widely used databases on financial reforms – the original index by Abiad et al. (2010) and its extension to 2015 by Denk and Gomes (2017) – to build a panel of seven dimensions of financial policy in 88 democracies from 1973 to 2015. The indices cover bank entry barriers, bank privatisation, banking supervision, credit controls, interest rate controls, capital account restrictions, and securities market regulation, each scaled between zero (fully repressed) and one (fully liberalised). We date banking, currency, and sovereign debt crises using the IMF database of Laeven and Valencia (2018), which yields 173 crisis episodes in our sample.

Our key political variable, taken from the Database of Political Institutions, indicates whether a country’s executive leader is serving their last legally allowed term. Crucially, this varies over time within countries: in a two-term system, for example, the same president is eligible for re-election in the first term but term-limited in the second. This lets us compare leaders within the same country, while controlling for country-specific trends in liberalisation and a rich set of fixed effects.

Lame ducks deliberalise after crises

Outside crisis periods, term-limited leaders and those eligible for re-election do not regulate finance differently. After a financial crisis, however, a sharp gap opens. Both types of leaders reverse financial liberalisation, but term-limited leaders do so to a much greater degree. Relative to the average level of the liberalisation index, a crisis reduces liberalisation by about 3% under a leader facing re-election, but by more than 9% under a term-limited leader – a roughly threefold difference. To put this into perspective, the additional postcrisis effect of a term limit is about 30% larger than the baseline effect of having a right-wing rather than a centrist government in power.

Figure 1 traces the timing of this effect. There is no differential behaviour in the years before a crisis, which is reassuring. After a crisis hits, the gap between the two types of leaders grows gradually and peaks three to four years after the crisis starts. 

Figure 1 Differential change in financial liberalisation under term-limited leaders around financial crises

Notes: The figure plots the estimated coefficients on the interaction between term limits and years relative to the start of a financial crisis. Bars show 90% confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the country level.
Source: Saka et al. (2026), Figure 3.

These results survive a battery of checks. They are unchanged when we control for how long the leader has been in office, the government’s vote share as a proxy for leaders’ ability, ideology, government fragmentation, and whether the country has a presidential or parliamentary system. They also hold when we include separate dummies for each of the 250 parties in power, ruling out the possibility that the rise of extreme parties after crises (Funke et al. 2016) drives the results. Dropping countries that never experienced a binding term limit during our sample makes the effect even stronger.

Incumbent banks benefit

Financial liberalisation is a broad umbrella with different winners and losers, so we zoom in on three banking policies where the interests of incumbent banks and the general public diverge most clearly. Higher entry barriers protect incumbent banks from competition at the expense of consumers, who face higher prices and lower service quality. Bank supervision is generally unwelcome to banks but valued by consumers. After crises, nationalisation typically takes the form of bailouts through equity injections into troubled banks – support that the industry welcomes but voters view with considerable scepticism.

In the wake of crises, term-limited leaders are significantly more likely than their re-election-eligible counterparts to raise barriers to entry into the banking sector and to nationalise banks. They also tend to relax bank supervision, although that effect is not statistically significant. Notably, leaders facing re-election do not behave differently after crises than in normal times in these domains. The gap therefore stems from what term-limited leaders do after crises rather than from voters disciplining those seeking re-election. Greater salience of financial policy, in other words, does not appear to be the main force at work.

Following the revolving door

Why would term-limited leaders favour banks after crises? We present three pieces of evidence pointing to quid pro quo relationships between policymakers and the financial industry.

First, the effect is much stronger where revolving doors between politics and finance are common. Using the measure of Braun and Raddatz (2010), who rank countries by how often former high-ranking politicians sit on bank boards, we split our sample in two. As Figure 2 shows, the post-crisis shift towards bank-friendly policies under term-limited leaders is almost three times larger in high revolving-door countries than in low revolving-door countries, and the difference between the two groups is statistically significant.

Figure 2 Postcrisis shift towards bank-friendly policies under term-limited leaders, by revolving-door intensity

Second, we follow the careers of more than 500 finance ministers and central bank governors in 32 democracies, using data compiled by Wirsching (2018). Officials who served under a term-limited leader in the aftermath of a crisis are about 30 percentage points more likely to take up a senior role – as president, board member, or adviser – in a private financial institution after leaving government. This is equivalent to more than three-quarters of the average probability of such a move. Serving under a term-limited leader or during a postcrisis period alone makes no difference: it is the combination that matters. Because our definition excludes state-owned institutions, the pattern is not a mechanical by-product of postcrisis nationalisations.

Third, a manual search of public records on the 106 term-limited leaders in our sample reveals that more than half had at least one link with their country’s financial industry – through paid roles after leaving office, cabinet members or officials with employment ties to banks, or corruption and family enrichment through the banking sector.

No gains for financial stability

One might argue that bank-friendly policies are exactly what a crisis calls for, and that the interests of banks and the public are aligned in the aftermath of a crisis. If so, banking sectors should perform better after crises when term-limited leaders are in charge. Using bank-level data from Bankscope covering 1999–2014, we find no evidence of this. Crises predictably weaken bank stability and performance across the board, but the policies pursued by term-limited leaders do not improve banks’ distance to default, profitability, or loan performance. The policies favoured by term-limited leaders do not deliver a more stable banking system.

Implications

Our findings suggest that crises are not uniformly good for reform. When electoral accountability is weak, crises can become opportunities to pass policies that benefit incumbent financial institutions at the expense of the public. The combination of a lame-duck leader, a crisis-induced legislative rush, and a well-trodden revolving door appears to be particularly potent.

This has implications for the design of institutions meant to keep policymakers accountable. Stricter cooling-off periods for senior officials moving into the financial sector, closer independent scrutiny of crisis-era financial legislation, and sunset clauses on emergency measures could all help narrow the windows of opportunity that crises open. More broadly, debates on term limits should recognise that their costs are not constant over time: they are likely to be highest precisely when the stakes for financial regulation are greatest.
